equation_request.abstract: We propose a method for implementation of an universal set of one- and two-quantum-bit gates for quantum computation in the system of two coupled electrons with constant non-diagonal exchange interaction. Suppression of the exchange interaction is offered to implement by all-the-time repetition of single spin rotations. Small g-factor difference of electrons allows to address qubits and to avoid strong magnetic field pulses. It is shown by means of numerical experiments that for implementation of one- and two-qubit operations it is sufficient to change the amplitude of the magnetic field within a few Gauss, introducing in a resonance one and then the other electron. To find the evolution of the two-qubit system, we use the algorithms of the optimal control theory.

specification.problem: Implement universal one- and two-qubit gates (e.g. single-qubit H/Rx on either electron, CNOT/CZ) on two exchange-coupled electron spins with constant exchange J and a small g-factor difference. Controls are a piecewise-constant static field amplitude within a few Gauss plus RF drive, found by optimal control. The simulator realizes this as a fixed 2-qubit Trotterized slice circuit with classically precomputed angles.
specification.reconstruction_scope: Smallest construction: 2 qubits, no ancillas. A model Hamiltonian with constant Heisenberg exchange and different Zeeman terms is split into N piecewise-constant slices. Each slice is Rz Zeeman, RXX/RYY/RZZ exchange, and Rx/Ry drive gates. Angles are optimized offline by GRAPE-like ascent for a target gate (CNOT or CZ) and hard-coded. Fidelity is judged on the unitary up to global phase, with an optional Bell-state check. Outside scope: the paper's actual parameter values, RWA derivation, the exact decoupling pulse sequence, and the numerical results.

static magnetic field amplitude, varied by a few Gauss
RF drive amplitude and phase in slice k

equations.label: Model Hamiltonian
equations.description: Two spins with different Zeeman splittings, constant Heisenberg exchange and a transverse RF drive that acts on both spins but is resonant with only one at a time. The Hamiltonian is the form given in the sketch; the exact normalization of J and the drive are assumptions.
equations.justification: The abstract names two coupled electrons, constant exchange, and a small g difference, but gives no explicit Hamiltonian.
assumptions: RF drive couples to both spins

equations.label: Selective resonance
equations.description: Changing B by a few Gauss brings one electron and then the other into resonance with the RF frequency, so the drive acts selectively.
equations.abstract_quote: Small g-factor difference of electrons allows to address qubits and to avoid strong magnetic field pulses.
equations.justification: Addressing via a small g difference implies different resonance conditions for the two spins. The selectivity inequality is my assumption.

equations.label: Slice product unitary
equations.description: The evolution is a product of piecewise-constant slice propagators. The circuit approximates each slice by a Trotter splitting into Rz, RXX/RYY/RZZ and Rx/Ry gates. XX, YY and ZZ commute, so the exchange factor is exact.
equations.justification: The abstract says optimal control finds the evolution; the slice parametrization follows the sketch.
assumptions: Trotter splitting error neglected or absorbed in the optimization

equations.label: Fidelity objective
equations.description: Phase-insensitive gate fidelity maximized by gradient ascent (GRAPE-style) to find the controls.
equations.abstract_quote: To find the evolution of the two-qubit system, we use the algorithms of the optimal control theory.
equations.justification: Optimal control implies maximizing a fidelity objective. The specific form is the standard one.

equations.label: Exchange suppression by refocusing
equations.description: The Heisenberg coupling is invariant under simultaneous rotations of both spins, so a common pi pulse does not refocus it. Suppression therefore needs spin-selective rotations, e.g. a pi pulse on one spin only, which flips the sign of the XX and YY parts. I flag this as a caveat on the sketch's dynamical decoupling claim, and the actual sequence is unspecified.
equations.justification: This is a fact about the Heisenberg interaction. It shows that the suppression sequence must be spin-selective and not a global pi pulse.

registers.name: q
registers.role: q0 = electron 1 spin, q1 = electron 2 spin; no ancillas

specification.initial_state: |00> for the unitary check. For the Bell test, apply H on q0 and then CNOT(q0,q1).

steps.description: Fix the target gate, N, \Delta t, and the J, g_1, g_2 values. Run GRAPE offline to obtain the slice angles and hard-code them.
Build the single-qubit selective rotations, with one electron resonant at a time via the B shift.
For each slice, apply the Rz Zeeman phases, the RXX/RYY/RZZ(J\Delta t/2) exchange, and the Rx/Ry drive gates, then concatenate the N slices.
Compare the unitary to U_target up to global phase via F. Optionally measure the Bell-state counts.

specification.measurement: Prefer the unitary or statevector with no measurements. For the optional Bell check, measure both qubits and expect correlated 00/11 outcomes.
specification.classical_postprocessing: Offline GRAPE optimization of the angles. Evaluate F(\theta) on the simulated unitary.
assumptions: Heisenberg exchange with J constant and always on
all numerical parameter values chosen by me
